items.title: Headlines for November 03, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## WSJ: U.S. Carries Out Strikes Around Strait of Hormuz on Eve of Midterm Elections Nov 03, 2026 In Iran, several explosions were reported overnight on Qeshm Island and in the port city of Bandar Lengeh, as The Wall Street Journal reported the U.S. had carried out strikes around the Strait of Hormuz. The attacks came on the eve of today’s midterm elections, which will determine the balance of power in the House and Senate, and just hours after President Trump declared that the U.S. is not at war with Iran. Trump spoke by phone with Fox News’s Sean Hannity. > President Donald Trump: “We’re not fighting a war. You know, everyone says, ’You’re at war!’ Well, when was the last time we fired anything? This isn’t a war. This is a very soft war.” The latest U.S. attacks on Iran came amid reports that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing for a massive wave of new strikes after today’s U.S. midterm elections. That could help Netanyahu form an emergency government, following his far-right coalition’s losses in last week’s elections in Israel. This comes as Iran’s Foreign Ministry said Monday it is prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days if the U.S. agrees to a set of demands. ## SCOTUS Rejects Trump Admin’s Attempt to Force California to Set Aside 20,000 Mail-In Ballots Nov 03, 2026 The Supreme Court has rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to force California to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots it claims may have come from noncitizens. On Monday, justices issued a short, unexplained order just hours after the Justice Department filed its emergency request. An analysis by UCLA researchers found the Trump administration flagged thousands of U.S. citizens as ineligible to vote, while more than 40% of the names provided could not even be found in California’s voter rolls. In a statement, California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta said, “This latest decision should put an end to the administration’s attempt to disrupt California’s elections through emergency court orders. But our work is not over. We will remain vigilant and keep fighting back against federal efforts to undermine our democracy.” ... ## Houthis Advance on Aden as Fighting Worsens Yemen’s Hunger Crisis In Yemen, fighters with the Ansar Allah movement known as the Houthis have advanced to within 50 miles of Aden, the temporary capital and main stronghold of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government. Saudi Arabia’s military responded with strikes on several Houthi-controlled regions that Ansar Allah says killed 10 people and injured dozens of others. Two of the airstrikes reportedly struck the University of Hodeidah’s medical school. Elsewhere, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted ballistic missiles and a drone fired by Ansar Allah toward southern Saudi Arabia. The fighting has exacerbated the hunger crisis in Yemen, where about three-quarters of households are unable to meet their basic daily food needs, according to the U.N. ... ## Russian Strike on Humanitarian Aid Center in Ukraine Leaves Dozens Injured or Dead Ukraine’s government says at least 31 people were killed and dozens of others remain missing after Russia bombed a humanitarian aid site in a village in Ukraine’s southern Zaporizhzhia region. Survivors called it a “double-tap” strike, with Russia first bombing a school building used to distribute aid, before a second wave of attacks on people at a nearby shelter. It’s one of the deadliest Russian strikes on civilians since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago. It came as Russia attacked nine regions of Ukraine overnight, triggering blackouts and injuring scores of people, including dozens of patients at a hospital in Kharkiv.

items.title: In top Senate race states, gas, grocery and housing costs are up
items.excerpt: Nov. 3, 2026, 7:44 AM EST By Alexandra Meier From gas and groceries to housing and wage growth, midterm voters who are being squeezed by inflation tell NBC News the economy is their top issue this Election Day. In 2024, President Donald Trump’s promise to bring down prices and make daily life more affordable helped him win back the White House. But nearly two years into his second term, Trump’s tariffs and his war with Iran have driven costs higher across the country, fueling deep discontent among voters. ... ## Pain at the pump In several of the states with close Senate races, voters face gas prices that have climbed higher, and more sharply, than the mean nationwide prices over the same period. Across the country, the average cost of a gallon of gas has risen 40% since Feb. 28, the day Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched attacks on Iran that sent crude oil prices through the roof. Right before the war, the average price of unleaded was $2.98 per gallon, according to NBC News’ gas price tracker. On Monday, it was $4.16. In Iowa, however, the average price has climbed by significantly more, nearly 55% since late February. The same figure applies in Nebraska. In Kansas, gas prices are up by 53%. ... Drivers in Michigan are also experiencing an outsized jump, with gas up 51% from $2.99 in February to $4.52 Monday. There, Democrat Abdul El Sayed is facing off against Republican Mike Rogers. In Ohio, where Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown is challenging incumbent Republican Jon Husted, the price of a gallon of gas has climbed by 48%. ... In Maine, the price of a gallon of gas is 46% higher than it was before the war, creating a drag on Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and an opportunity for Democrat Troy Jackson. Even when national average gas prices pivot lower, as they did throughout October, that doesn’t always extend to parts of the country where refinery activity influences fuel costs, particularly in the Great Lakes region. Far from the coasts, refineries that service Michigan, Ohio and Iowa cannot easily restore supply lost to weather events or refinery capacity. “When you’re isolated in the interior of the country, these problems can linger as long as the refinery is experiencing issues,” said Patrick De Haan, chief petroleum analyst at GasBuddy. ... Beyond the gas pump, voters are also feeling the sting of higher oil prices overseas in the form of increased transportation costs for groceries and retail goods. In several of the states with tight Senate races, average households are spending a lot more of their monthly income on groceries than shoppers elsewhere in the country, according to a WalletHub study. ... ## Your money buys you less While Americans are technically earning more in dollar terms on average, paychecks are not keeping up with the pace of inflation. Wages in September grew by 3.0% year over year. But the annual inflation rate hit 3.7%. Adjusting for inflation, this means average hourly earnings nationwide fell by about 0.7%. This disparity is another source of economic pressure on voters going into Election Day. But the gap between wage growth and inflation is significantly wider in some of the states that will be most closely watched Tuesday night. In Nebraska, purchasing power fell by 3.5% over the three months ending in August, relative to regional inflation. Iowa saw a drop of 2.6%. And in Alaska, real pay fell by 2.0% compared to the same period last year.

items.excerpt: ## A consumer this healthy keeps inflation sticky "Core PCE inflation is supposed to be 2%," Sløk wrote in a Nov. 1 note. "Unfortunately, it has been 3% for three years, and it is now moving higher." Core PCE, the Fed's favorite inflation gauge, rose 3.1% in September from a year earlier and hasn't dipped to 2% since early 2021. Sløk estimated last week that about half of that inflation now comes from strong demand, the part higher interest rates can actually help cool down. So how much cooling would it take? A lot. His model says the Fed would need to lift its benchmark rate to roughly 6.75% by the end of 2027, he wrote in a Nov. 2 note. That's nearly 3 percentage points above today's 3.75%-4% range and would be the highest since January 1991. ... The Fed "may be further from its inflation goal than the market currently expects," Sløk wrote. The next clue arrives with Friday's October jobs report, which will show whether hiring is still strong enough to keep a December rate hike on the table.

Crude oil prices fell Tuesday for a second consecutive session, as the market hopes the U.S. and Iran will reach a diplomatic settlement to the conflict that has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months. U.S. West Texas Intermediate Add To Watchlist futures lost 37 cents to close at $96.09 a barrel after dipping below $95 earlier in the session. Brent crude Add To Watchlist, the international benchmark, shed $1.17 to settle at $103.60. The move lower came after rumors circulated the U.S. and Iran were making progress toward a deal. Oil sold off more than 7% on Monday after Washington and Tehran signaled they were both open to discussions to reach a settlement. President Donald Trump told reporters Tehran wants "to make a deal and that could happen." Qatar is continuing to mediate talks between the U.S. and Iran, the Gulf state's foreign ministry said Tuesday. A delegation from Qatar held talks in Tehran in an effort to reach an agreement that prevents further escalation in the region and ends the U.S.-Iran conflict, the foreign ministry said. However, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Emsaeil Baqaei said Tuesday that Tehran will not accept diplomacy based on coercion, according to the state-owned media outlet Islamic Republic News Agency. It was unclear where talks actual stand. ... items.title: U.S. Economy Grows 3.4% as 3.7% Inflation Keeps Costs in Focus | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: The U.S. economy expanded at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, while inflation reached 3.7% over the year through September as voters prepared to weigh economic conditions in Tuesday’s midterm elections. ... The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) estimated real gross domestic product (GDP) grew at a 3.4% annual rate from July through September, compared with 2.2% in the second quarter. Investment, consumer spending and government spending contributed to the gain; lower exports partly offset it as imports increased. BEA data show real personal consumption expenditures grew at a 3.8% annual rate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.6% in September from August and 3.7% over the 12 months through September. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, increased 0.3% for the month and 2.6% over the year. The CPI gasoline index climbed 9.1% in September, accounting for more than half of that month’s increase in the overall index. Annual inflation had fallen from 9.1% in June 2022 to 2.3% in April 2025 before rising again; the lower rate meant prices were rising more slowly, not falling overall.

items.title: Republicans fight to hold on to the Senate as Democrats seek gains in traditionally red states
items.excerpt: Control of the Senate is on the line Tuesday, following a midterm election cycle with races marked by betrayal, alleged ballot shenanigans and President Donald Trump’s incessant swooning over the backside of one Republican candidate. Close races are expected in several traditional battlegrounds — including Georgia, Michigan and North Carolina — but also in states that have become more reliably red since Trump’s rise in politics, such as Ohio and Iowa. There also are closer-than-expected races brewing in even redder states such as Alaska, Kansas and Texas. Underscoring the high stakes: More than $3.4 billion has been spent on television and digital advertisements in Senate races across the country, according to tracking firm AdImpact. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the chamber, meaning Democrats would need a net gain of four seats to regain control. The consequences for Trump are significant. For the past two years, his own Republican Party has controlled both chambers of Congress, allowing him to pursue his agenda largely unchecked. But if the Republicans lose the Senate, he’ll need Democratic cooperation to move forward on legislation and appointments. Democrats will have increased power to pursue investigations into the administration. Alaska has emerged late as a closely watched contest. Democrat Mary Peltola is under scrutiny after a New York Times report that her campaign and other Democrats recruited a candidate into the race — Dan J. Sullivan — with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The “ballot-stacking” tactic is seen as a way to sow confusion among voters in a state that uses ranked choice voting and has four Senate candidates on the ballot.

items.title: Top Ent News Nov 3: Alia Bhatt, Neetu Kapoor Grace Ramayana Premiere; Armaan Malik Reacts To Mangal Rang Row | Bollywood News - News18
items.excerpt: With just two days left for its theatrical release, the excitement around Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana: Part One is building. The makers are hosting a special screening for the film’s cast, crew, and invited guests from the film industry in Mumbai today, November 3. The event is being held at an IMAX theatre in Lower Parel, ahead of the grand release on November 5. Alia Bhatt and Neetu Kapoor were seen arriving in style to cheer for Ranbir Kapoor, who will be seen playing Lord Rama’s role in the film. The track, Mangal Rang, from Ramayana: Rise Of A Legend has sparked a debate over its musical treatment. Critics have stated that the composition carries Sufi-qawwali influences and seems culturally misplaced in a film based on the Hindu epic. Many others have also compared it to AR Rahman’s earlier songs, particularly Kun Faya Kun from Rockstar and Enna Solla Pogirai, accusing him of recycling familiar musical patterns. Speaking exclusively to News18, Armaan Malik, who has lent his vocals to the Kannada version of Mangal Rang titled Mangala Sangama alongside Bela Shende, reacts to the debate.

items.title: AP Entertainment SummaryBrief at 8:11 a.m. EST | Entertainment | wvnews.com
items.excerpt: - Nov 3, 2026 ... Movie Review: In 'Godzilla Minus Zero,' human-scaled melodrama stomps out the kaiju fun Even Godzilla can be felled by an old hazard: the sophomore slump. Though Godzilla has been stomping around for more than half a century, “Godzilla Minus Zero” is a sequel. It follows the quite excellent, Oscar-winning “Godzilla Minus One,” a reset for the kaiju franchise that brought Godzilla back to its postwar Japan roots. Like its predecessor, the follow-up marries human-scaled drama with a flair for stompy-stomp spectacle. Yet AP Film Writer Jake Coyle says those calibrations are slightly off in “Godzilla Minus Zero.” In his review, Coyle writes that the melodrama on the ground overtakes the movie, sagging it with a bloated story that leaves you pining for the big guy to turn up again. NEW YORK (AP) — David Mendizábal is directing a revival of Lin-Manuel Miranda’s "In the Heights," a musical that was Mendizábal's introduction to theater. The show, running for three weeks at New York City Center, features a new cast of Latino artists. Mendizábal emphasizes the importance of showcasing Latino communities, especially now. Miranda, who starred in the original production, reflects on the musical's enduring relevance. The revival comes amid immigration tensions, highlighting themes of gentrification and community. New and old cast members say the musical remains a celebration of the Latino immigrant experience, with its messages resonating strongly today. NEW YORK (AP) — My Chemical Romance has hit No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with “The Black Parade (20th Anniversary Deluxe Edition).” This reissue of their 2006 rock opera includes six bonus tracks. Back then, it debuted at No. 2 due to competition from Disney’s “Hannah Montana” soundtrack. The reissue's success is driven by 20 physical variants and a significant increase in album sales. The band’s reunion and anniversary tour have also fueled interest. Nostalgic fans and new listeners are connecting with the album's unique style and themes. This marks the longest wait for an album to reach No. 1. WASHINGTON (AP) — The Kennedy Center has announced that Paul Anka, David Foster, Andy Garcia, David Mamet and Barbara Mandrell will be honored at this year's Kennedy Center Honors. The event will take place away from the iconic venue for the first time due to President Donald Trump's legal battle over renovations and naming rights. The nominees have had substantial careers in their fields. Mamet is a renowned playwright, while Mandrell is a Country Music Hall of Fame member. Anka, a longtime friend of Trump, has rewritten “My Way” with MAGA-themed lyrics. The ceremony will be held on December 7 at Washington's Capital One Arena.

items.title: Movie News: 3rd November 2026
items.excerpt: ### Wicker’s UK number one, Clayface’s quiet global win, Jailer 2 breaks ₹800 crore, Marrakech’s line-up, the AFM, Iceman casting & Carrie turns 50. ... UK and Ireland box office: Black Bear’s Wicker had the first number one film in its distributor’s history, opening to £1.7 million from 676 cinemas, a £2,515 average, which rises to £1.8 million including previews. A24’s Primetime, starring Robert Pattinson as To Catch a Predator‘s paedo-hunting host Chris Hansen, opened in third place with £1.3 million from 560 cinemas, a £2,321 average, and £1.7 million with previews. Clayface dropped 37% in its second weekend to £1.2 million, taking it to £4.7 million. It’s a Halloween weekend for the re-releases, too, with Pan’s Labyrinth in 384 cinemas, Donnie Darko in 202 and Ken Russell’s The Devils in 73 in a new 4K restoration from BFI Distribution. The weekend box office, worldwide: Clayface topped the worldwide chart for a second weekend with an estimated $22.8 million, which is dismally low for a chart-topping film, as a lack of significant new releases over Halloween weekend left the market becalmed. The UK and Ireland is its biggest international market, with $6.1 million to date. Laika’s astounding Wildwood moved up to second place after international expansion, and Wicker was seventh with a $7 million start, made up of $4.1 million from North America and $2.6 million from nine international markets. In the UK, Wicker‘s opening beat those of Poor Things and The Shape of Water, according to Deadline. Elsewhere, Resident Evil has now passed $400 million worldwide. In North America, yesterday’s estimates have been confirmed, and You Can See Everything came out on top with $11.4 million in its third weekend, a little higher than expected, ahead of Clayface with $11 million. Clayface now has $44.6 million in North America and $83 million worldwide, while the whole weekend came in at roughly $60 million, one of the slowest of the year. Tamil cinema: Jailer 2 breaks ₹800 crore: Rajinikanth’s Jailer 2 passed ₹800 crore worldwide on its 18th day, finishing its third weekend with a worldwide gross of ₹807.25 crore (about $84 million), according to Sacnilk. It’s the first Tamil film to pass both ₹700 crore and ₹800 crore, and it now stands as the highest-grossing Tamil film ever and reportedly the second-highest-grossing Indian film of 2026. It has earned ₹456.3 crore net in India (about $48 million) and ₹273.5 crore (about $28 million) overseas, and it added ₹26.4 crore net in India over its third weekend. The Far East: Resident Evil’s China hold: In mainland China, Resident Evil was number one for a fourth consecutive weekend with RMB 28.5 million ($4.3 million), taking it to $71.3 million since its 5 October opening. The crime drama Traces of Justice remains ahead overall with $98.5 million since 1 October. The wider market had a quiet weekend with $18.2 million, and the year-to-date total of $4.73 billion is down 29.0% on 2025. A 2014 re-release of John Wick opened in third place. Marrakech’s line-up: The 23rd Marrakech International Film Festival, which runs from 20 to 28 November, has unveiled a line-up of 76 films from 39 countries, including 10 world premieres. As I mentioned when it closed the London Film Festival, Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut opens the festival, and Marion Cotillard presides over the competition jury. Gala screenings include Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial and James Gray’s Paper Tiger, and 14 films compete for the Étoile d’Or, including Yoon Dan-bi’s The World Before and Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo’s Ben’imana. The American Film Market gets going: Hockey’s Hollywood moment, largely driven by the success of Heated Rivalry, has reached the AFM, with Liam Neeson set to play a legendary coach in Believe 13, about his bond with an injured high school star. Closer to home, Guy Pearce, Sabrina Impacciatore, Rachael Stirling and Selena Tan have joined Jeff Daniels in Trudie Styler’s The Reception, a chaotic wedding-party comedy that’s currently shooting on location in Scotland. Iceman casting: Ben Wang, the star of Karate Kid: Legends, who also plays District 12 tribute Wyatt Callow in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping on 20 November, is in talks to play Iceman in Marvel’s X-Men reboot, which Jake Schreier is directing for 2028. The deal isn’t done, and Gabriel LaBelle, Jackson Kelly and Rhenzy Feliz all reportedly tested for the part. It would leave Beast as the only member of the original team without an actor, and the casting news arrives just days after Patrick Stewart’s farewell as Professor X was confirmed.
